name: Sextant Shoals

stars.name: Sextant
stars.notes: A young, brilliant white star that pours out ultraviolet and attitude in equal measure; navigators prize its sharp limb for sights and give its radiation belts a wide berth.

planets.name: Glare
planets.notes: A radiation-flensed cinder so close to Sextant that its surface re-anneals each perihelion; probes last minutes here, and the record is eleven.

planets.name: Whetstone
planets.notes: A glass-fused rockball where the starlight has welded the regolith smooth; a lone prospector's beacon still blinks on its nightside, unowned since the claimant vanished.

planets.name: Grand Arc
planets.notes: A young giant still glowing with collapse heat, wrapped in fast-shifting storm arcs; it shepherds the outer shoal of debris and anchors every sight taken in this system.

asteroid_belts.name: The Long Shoal
asteroid_belts.notes: A scattered shoal of comet nuclei and dirty ice stretching out into dark; survey drones pick their way through it the way sailors once read water.

faction_control.notes: Two consortiums hold overlapping paper claims to the shoal's ice, but neither maintains so much as a beacon crew; the only permanent presence is one robot observatory parked in orbit of Grand Arc by an amateur astronomy collective.

history: Charted during the first great triangulation of the Graticule Expanse, when survey crews used Grand Arc's crisp limb for sextant-style fixes and named the system for the instrument they missed.
An automated assessment a century ago confirmed what the glare already suggested: radiation levels preclude easy settlement, and the file was closed with unusual speed even for its era.

Last year, amateur astronomers noticed Grand Arc's storm arcs migrating faster than any model predicts, prompting the collective to park a single robot observatory in orbit; its data feed is public, sporadic, and oddly popular.
description: A fierce white star burns over three worlds: a flensed cinder, a whetted stone, and a young giant still warm from its own formation, trailing a sparse shoal of ice into the outer dark. Everything here is either too hot, too cold, or too radioactive, usually all three depending on the hour.

Nobody lives in Sextant Shoals and nothing is mined from it, which makes it rare among systems on any chart. Minimal traffic consists of drone tenders servicing the observatory and the occasional racer cutting close to Sextant's limb for a calibration sight no other star can provide. The two consortiums that hold claims visit about once a decade, mostly to renew paperwork.

The mystery worth watching sits at Grand Arc: storm arcs are rearranging faster than physics comfortably allows, and the little observatory's public feed recently began including frames nobody admits to adding — long-exposure shots in which the giant's arcs appear to form angles too regular to be weather. The collective says it is compression artifacting. The collective has said so four times now, each time slightly less confidently.
